title: Rotate a leaked secret
summary: What to do the moment a password, API key or token was exposed (committed to Git, written to a log, pasted in a chat): replace it, check whether it was misused, and report it as a security incident when it was.

resources.title: Rotation guide per secret type
resources.description: Step by step for database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens and certificates.

resources.title: Skill: rotate a secret
resources.description: Creates the new version in Secret Manager and opens the pull requests that switch services to it.

prerequisites.title: Access to the secret in Secret Manager
prerequisites.description: You need the 'secret admin' group of the project that holds the secret. Security can rotate it for you if you do not have it.

actors.name: You
actors.description: Whoever noticed the leak or owns the secret.

actors.name: Cyber Security
actors.description: Slack #security, out of hours via PagerDuty 'security-on-call'.

actors.name: Secret scanner
actors.description: Scans repositories and logs for secrets.

steps.title: Tell Cyber Security straight away
steps.description: Do this before anything else, even if you are not sure the secret is real. Do not post the secret itself.
instructions: Post in #security: what kind of secret, where it was exposed and since when.
Out of hours, page 'security-on-call' in PagerDuty.

steps.title: Create a new version of the secret
instructions: Generate a new value at the provider (database, API, cloud key).
Add it as a new version in Secret Manager; do not delete the old version yet.

steps.title: Switch every service to the new secret
instructions: Find every service that reads the secret (search the deployment files for its name).
Point them at the new version or restart them if they read the latest version.

steps.title: Revoke the old secret
instructions: Revoke or disable the old value at the provider.
Disable the old version in Secret Manager.

steps.title: Remove the secret from where it leaked
steps.description: Removing it does not make it safe again - that is why it is revoked first - but it stops others copying it.
instructions: Delete the chat message, log entries or ticket comment that contain it.
For Git: ask #devex to purge it from the history; a new commit is not enough.

steps.title: Check whether the secret was used by someone else
steps.description: Security reads the access logs of the provider for the time the secret was exposed.

steps.title: Raise a security incident
steps.description: Handled like any production incident, with Cyber Security as incident commander.

steps.title: Scan again for the old secret
steps.description: The scanner checks repositories and the log platform once more for the old value.

steps.title: Write down how it leaked
instructions: In the #security thread, write in three sentences how the secret was exposed.
Name one change that stops it happening again, e.g. a pre-commit secret scan.
